steps: Assume T := closure of phi'(g) + chi'(g) is self-adjoint and affiliated to M', A is in M, and Psi, Phi are finite-particle vectors in Dom(T).
Since T is affiliated to M' and A is in M, A commutes strongly with T, so A Dom(T) is contained in Dom(T) and T A = A T on Dom(T).
Because A Phi lies in Dom(T) and T is self-adjoint, <T Psi, A Phi> = <Psi, T A Phi> for the vectors Psi, Phi in Dom(T).
Using T A Phi = A T Phi on Dom(T), <Psi, T A Phi> = <Psi, A T Phi> = <A^* Psi, T Phi>, so <T Psi, A Phi> = <A^* Psi, T Phi>.
Substituting T Psi = phi'(g) Psi + chi'(g) Psi and T Phi = phi'(g) Phi + chi'(g) Phi into <T Psi, A Phi> = <A^* Psi, T Phi> and rearranging the four terms.
Hence <phi'(g) Psi, A Phi> - <A^* Psi, phi'(g) Phi> = -[ <chi'(g) Psi, A Phi> - <A^* Psi, chi'(g) Phi> ], with chi'(g) acting only on the chosen vectors Psi and Phi.
The form identity for the chi'-corrected commutator therefore holds without any domain condition requiring A Phi or A^* Psi to lie in Dom(chi'(g)).

traps.text: Write the chi'-part as <Psi, [chi'(g), A] Phi>, with chi'(g) acting to the right on A Phi, and require A Phi, A^* Psi in Dom(chi'(g)).
traps.why: This imposes domain condition (D), which every explicit vector in the programme violates; the form reading never needs it.

traps.text: Conclude that the two chi'-terms of the identity sit on the same contour line Im w = -pi/3.
traps.why: The term with chi' on Psi carries the conjugate of g^+, which lives on the line Im w = -2 pi/3, so there are two lines.

steps: The one-particle reflected bound-state operator acts as (chi'_1(g) xi)(theta) = eta g^+(theta - i pi/3) xi(theta + i pi/3), with eta = sqrt(2 pi |R|) and g real supported in W_R.
In the pairing <A^* Psi, chi'(g) Phi> the test-function factor enters as g^+ evaluated on the line Im w = -pi/3, so this term pairs g^+ on that line.
In the pairing <chi'(g) Psi, A Phi> the factor g^+(t - i pi/3) enters complex conjugated, because chi'(g) Psi sits in the antilinear slot of the inner product.
For real g supported in W_R, on the real axis g^+(theta - i pi) = g^-(theta) = conj(g^+(theta)), and analytic continuation of this relation gives conj(g^+(t - i pi/3)) = g^+(t - 2 i pi/3) for real t.
Hence the pairing <chi'(g) Psi, A Phi> pairs g^+ on the line Im w = -2 pi/3, while <A^* Psi, chi'(g) Phi> pairs g^+ on the line Im w = -pi/3.
In the variable zeta = w + i pi used for (A Omega)_n, the two lines Im w = -pi/3 and Im w = -2 pi/3 become Im zeta = 2 pi/3 and Im zeta = pi/3.
The heights Im zeta = pi/3 and Im zeta = 2 pi/3 are exactly the two fusion poles of S, so the continued function has jump lines at both fusion heights and nowhere else in the first step.

traps.text: Conclude that the continuation has a single jump line Im w = -pi/3 and that poles seen at the second fusion height are an artefact of the test class.
traps.why: The conjugated half of the form commutator produces the second line Im w = -2 pi/3 automatically (Lane B2a's unexplained Fact 2).

traps.text: Conclude that the chi' contribution cancels the fusion residue so the continued function is analytic across the strip.
traps.why: The record finds no cancellation: the residue is supplied by the chi'-kernel and the continuation is meromorphic with simple poles.

steps: The two jump densities of the residue-corrected continuation are M'_2(t) = <Y'(t) Psi, A Phi> and M'_1(t) = <A^* Psi, Y'(t) Phi>, with Psi, Phi fixed finite-particle test vectors and A in M.
Componentwise, |<Y'(t) Psi, X>| <= eta n sup_t ||Psi_n( . , t + i pi/3)|| times ||X_n( . , t)|| for any vector X, where eta = sqrt(2 pi |R|).
Taking X = A Phi and applying Cauchy-Schwarz in t gives ||M'_2||_2 <= eta n C(Psi) ||A Phi||, where C(Psi) is the height-pi/3 sup-of-slices constant of Psi.
Since ||A Phi|| <= ||A|| ||Phi|| for the bounded operator A in M, ||M'_2||_2 <= eta n C(Psi) ||A|| ||Phi||.
By the same argument with the roles of the two test vectors exchanged, ||M'_1||_2 <= eta n C(Phi) ||A|| ||Psi||.
Both jump densities are bounded in L^2 by a constant times ||A||, the constant depending only on the chosen test vectors, which are finite for Schwartz-class one-particle data.

traps.text: Bound the term <Psi, Y(theta) A Phi> by edge L^2 norms of g^+ applied to the vector A Phi.
traps.why: Edge norms of g^+ do not control the interior line Im = -pi/3 for A Phi; this is Lane B2b's uniformity leak, closed only by moving Y' onto Psi.

traps.text: Apply the same uniform bound with Psi, Phi taken to be Lechner's S-symmetrized product states.
traps.why: For product states the height-pi/3 sup of slices is infinite (Lane D Cor D4), so the constant C blows up and the leak reopens.

steps: On the explicit polynomial class A = phi~(f_1) phi~(f_2) phi~(f_3) with ordered supports, the computed s-channel residue at n = 3 equals c'_3 times the TAGGED part of (A Omega)_2, not c'_3 times the full (A Omega)_2.
The form identity of Proposition E.1 and the continuation Lemma E.2 require A to be a bounded element of M commuting strongly with the self-adjoint field phi~'(g).
A polynomial A = phi~(f_1) phi~(f_2) in the unbounded fields is itself an unbounded operator, so it is not an element of the von Neumann algebra M.
Moving phi~'(g) past the second factor of phi~(f_1) phi~(f_2) would need phi~(f_2) Omega in Dom(phi~'(g)), which fails, so the polynomial does not commute strongly with phi~'(g).
Hence Lemma E.2 makes no prediction for the polynomial class, and the tagged residue found there is consistent with, not evidence against, Lemma E.2 for genuine A in M.
The hypothesis of Proposition E.1 that fails on the polynomial class is therefore membership A in M, not the domain condition (D) on A Phi and A^* Psi.

traps.text: Account for the untagged deficit of the s-channel residue by adding the t-channel residue at the second fusion height.
traps.why: Checked numerically at five points: the ratio of the t-channel residue to the deficit varies with no constant, so it does not account for it.

traps.text: Conclude from the polynomial-class numerics that for genuine A in M the jump densities are only the tagged parts.
traps.why: The polynomial class is not in M, so the full-versus-tagged density question for genuine A stays an untested conjecture.

steps: Lechner's evaluation tube for (A Omega)_n is centred at lambda_0 = (-pi/2, ..., -pi/2) with a cube C_n(kappa) of half-width kappa/2 in each imaginary coordinate.
On a tube centred at a diagonal point with half-width kappa/2 per coordinate, the imaginary part of every rapidity difference theta_k - theta_j ranges over the open interval (-kappa, kappa).
Take as given that the polar set of (A Omega)_n lies inside the hyperplanes where Im(theta_k - theta_j) belongs to (pi/6)Z minus {0}.
Since the imaginary parts of rapidity differences stay inside (-kappa, kappa) on Lechner's tube, the tube avoids every hyperplane Im(theta_k - theta_j) in (pi/6)Z minus {0} whenever kappa < pi/6.
The single pole-free block f_{-B/3} of the Bullough-Dodd S has its nearest singularity below the real axis at -i pi/6, so its regularity collar kappa(S_2) is exactly pi/6.

Therefore the pole-carrying S with chi and the single pole-free Lechner block use the same collar pi/6, and their Section 5 estimates differ only through sup |S| on the collar and the chi inflation factor.

traps.text: Attribute the factor of about 2 in s_0, relative to a fictitious pole-free S with collar pi/2, to the cost of the pole and chi.
traps.why: The factor is a collar artefact: the genuine pole-free block with collar pi/6 gives the same s_0 to under 1 percent.

steps: Let (M, U, Omega) be a Borchers triple with Omega cyclic and separating for M, modular operator Delta and modular conjugation J, so the Tomita operator J Delta^{1/2} maps A Omega to A^* Omega for A in M.
Since J is antiunitary, for A in M one has ||Delta^{1/2} A Omega|| = ||J Delta^{1/2} A Omega|| = ||A^* Omega|| <= ||A^*|| = ||A||.
By the spectral theorem ||Delta^{1/4} A Omega||^2 = <A Omega, Delta^{1/2} A Omega>, and Cauchy-Schwarz gives ||Delta^{1/4} A Omega||^2 <= ||A Omega|| ||Delta^{1/2} A Omega||.
Combining ||A Omega|| <= ||A|| with ||Delta^{1/2} A Omega|| <= ||A|| yields ||Delta^{1/4} A Omega|| <= ||A|| for every A in M.
For translations s with Ad U(s) M contained in M, U(s) A Omega = U(s) A U(s)^* Omega by translation invariance of Omega, and U(s) A U(s)^* lies in M with the same norm as A.
Hence the modular map Xi(s): A -> Delta^{1/4} U(s) A Omega satisfies ||Xi(s) A|| <= ||A||, so ||Xi(s)|| <= 1, without any Bisognano-Wichmann input.

traps.text: Upgrade the abstract contraction bound ||Xi(s)|| <= 1 to nuclearity of Xi(s) on the n >= 2 particle sectors using only abstract modular data.
traps.why: The record proves abstract data cannot give nuclearity for n >= 2: the operator is decomposable over relative rapidities and not compact.

steps: In Lechner's tube coordinates zeta = theta - i lambda, the step-k flat piece E_2 has zeta_j = theta_j - i pi for j <= k, zeta_{k+1} = theta_{k+1} - i lambda_{k+1}, and zeta_j = theta_j real for j >= k+2.
On E_2 the dependence on zeta_{k+1} comes from S-factors and from the commutator matrix element, whose continuation has simple poles at zeta_{k+1} = theta_j - i c with c in {pi/3, 2 pi/3}.
For an index j >= k+2, where zeta_j = theta_j is real, the pole zeta_{k+1} = theta_j - i c lies on the hyperplane Im(zeta_{k+1} - zeta_j) = -c.
For an index j <= k, where zeta_j = theta_j - i pi, the pole zeta_{k+1} = theta_j - i c gives zeta_j - zeta_{k+1} = -i (pi - c), so Im(zeta_j - zeta_{k+1}) = -(pi - c).
Since c and pi - c both lie in {pi/3, 2 pi/3}, every pole at step k sits on a hyperplane Im(zeta_a - zeta_b) in {-pi/3, -2 pi/3} with a < b.
Hence every pole of every induction step lies on P_n^ord, the union over a < b of the fusion hyperplanes Im(zeta_a - zeta_b) = -pi/3 or -2 pi/3 in the ordered chamber.

traps.text: Apply the Malgrange-Zerner flat tube theorem directly to the convolved function (A Omega)_n * f.
traps.why: The poles lie inside the open flat piece E_2 at lambda_{k+1} = pi/3, 2 pi/3, and the theorem needs analyticity on both flat pieces.

traps.text: Subtract the poles, run the induction on the regular part of the convolved function, and add the poles back at the end.
traps.why: Convolution turns each point pole into a Cauchy-transform line jump, and the subtracted residues would need continuation where they have their own poles.
